content:
Author

: Philippe Chanial

Title

: Proudhon, Sociologist and Activist of the Autonomy of the Social

Date

: 2017

Notes

: Translated by Shaun Murdock.

Source

: “Proudhon, sociologue et militant de l’autonomie du social” Revue de la Société P.-J. Proudhon, no. 3 (2017): 9–16. Source in French: 

https://www.proudhon.net/philippe-chanial-proudhon-sociologue-et-militant-de-lautonomie-du-social/




 If Proudhon can and should be read as a forerunner of sociology, is it not above all because he was one of the first to have systematically hypothesised the autonomy of its very object, the “social”? As everyone knows, this hypothesis is foundational to sociology. The late Pierre Ansart reminded us that the heart of Proudhon’s sociological thesis is an “essential heterogeneity of the social relative to the individual”.

[1]

 Before him, the Durkheimian Célestin Bouglé emphasised that if Proudhon’s work pertains to sociological theory, it is because it shares the premise that “the meeting of individual entities generates an original reality, something greater than and different to their mere sum”. And, he continued, “arguably no thinker has made greater use of this premise than Proudhon” because “he constantly opposes, to purely individual phenomena, the notions of collective force, collective being and collective reason”.

[2]




 However, this theory of the irreducibility of the social – of the collective – to the individual does not exhaust this hypothesis of the autonomy of the social. It raises another question: that of the relationship between the social, the political and the economic. In the war of the sciences, sociology was only able to assert itself as an autonomous science by rejecting the self-proclaimed status of both political philosophy and political economy as the science of society.

[3]

 It did so by refusing that the mystery of the social order – the fact that there is, among or between people, something rather than nothing (chaos, arbitrary violence, war of all against all, etc.) or, to put it another way, the fact that people manage to give a lasting form to their coexistence – can be resolved either by identifying society with a system of power, as if the heteronomy of its political establishment, even if it were legitimate, were the absolute condition for the possibility of human coexistence; or by reducing it to a market, as if commercial ties alone were sufficient to make society. But is it not this double refusal that also defines the unique anarchism and socialism of Proudhon? Is is not this hypothesis of an autonomy of the social that enables both sociology as a scientific discipline, and socialism or anarchism as paths for emancipation? 




 Let us therefore attempt to unravel some of the simultaneously sociological and normative questions raised by this Proudhonian plea for an autonomy of the social. 




The irreducibility of the social to the political and the economic




 In his Carnets of 1852, Proudhon said: “I do politics to kill it. To put an end to politics.” This confession summarises, in a particularly polemical tone, his well-known critique of governmentalism. But this desire to end the “governmental bias” should not be reduced to a purely negative injunction to abolish all powers. It is also an invitation to accede to a “constitution of society” that is no longer based on the hierarchy of political powers but on the free organisation of social forces. It is in 

Confessions of a Revolutionary

, written, as Pierre Ansart also recalled, “in a sort of anger after the failure of a hoped-for social revolution”

[4]

, that Proudhon makes this fundamental distinction: 




 “In every society I find the distinction between two kinds of constitution, one of which I call the 

social

 constitution and the other the 

political

 constitution; the first, inherent to humanity, liberal, necessary, the development of which consists above all in weakening and gradually eliminating the second, which is essentially factitious, restrictive and transitory. The social constitution is nothing but the equilibrium of interests founded upon free 

contract

 and the organisation of 

economic forces

, which are in general: Labour, Division of Labour, Collective Force, Competition, Commerce, Money, Machines, Credit, Property, Equality in transactions, Reciprocity of guarantees, etc. The political constitution has 

authority

 as its principle. Its forms are: Class Distinctions, Separation of Powers, Administrative Centralisation, Judicial Hierarchy [...]. These two constitutions are [...] of utterly different and even incompatible natures”.

[5]




 This fit of anger is also a theoretical and normative act of force, as if society could – and should – no longer be established on the basis of political heteronomy but on the autonomy of the social, on the mutual guarantee of the liberty of all by all, which on the contrary allows us, under the supreme law of justice and contract, to do without any government. By this radical gesture, Proudhon can thus be interpreted, inseparably, as a pioneer of anarchism but also of sociology. Indeed, while Proudhon constantly suggests that it is necessary to “proceed [...] to social reform through the extermination of power and politics”, such a reform, in all its radicality, assumes a science of the social (which he calls for as early as 

The Celebration of Sunday

 in 1839) capable of asserting that the social order – and Proudhon also continues to advocate for order – is an immanent order: an order that precedes the political order, and that cannot therefore proceed from it. In this sense, this new science requires dethroning political philosophy in its age-old ambition to constitute “the” science of society, in order to better assert the primacy of the “social constitution” over the “political constitution”.

 THE great events which are creating such an excitement in the West Indies over the last shreds of the ancient colonial empire of Spain will undoubtedly have consequences of extreme importance, and become, in the fullest sense of the term, a part of history. But, however intense their interest, and however marked the change which they are certain to occasion in the equilibrium of the world, they remain altogether inferior in real significance to the revolutions which are taking place in the Far East. 




 War of some sort between America and Spain on the subject of Cuba had long been unavoidable. No less than a century ago, — at the time when France lost her plantations in San Domingo, and the republic of Hayti was born, — it was easy to foresee the rupture of the ties which had bound to the Spain of Cortez and Pizarro the insular fragments of the great hemisphere appropriated by Pope Alexander VI. The various colonies were sure to break away, one by one, from their metropolitan stepmother, set up for themselves, and live their own life. Cuba and Porto Rico, sucked into the whirlpool of war, are but accomplishing their “manifest destiny,” and fulfilling the prophecies repeatedly uttered by the historians of the last generation but one. 




 The progress of events in the eastern portion of the Asian continent had by no means been so fully anticipated. One might certainly have ventured to predict that there, also, populations long crushed by civil and military oppression would one day lay claim to the rights of free men; but it could never have been foreseen under what amazingly dramatic conditions the claim would be asserted. Our ancestors, at the beginning of the nineteenth century, would never have harbored, in their wildest dreams, the fantastic notion that Japan, the empire of the Rising Sun, would spontaneously transform itself into a “European power;” European, at least, if not in language, history, and traditions, in the complete recasting of its administration, institutions, customs, and theories, in its devotion to science, and in its entire and unreserved acceptance of a policy based on observation and experience. 




 This is the great event of the century, — one which casts into the shade all the other occurrences of an epoch which has nevertheless been rich in memorable events. And it will be no solitary 

avatar;

 there are unmistakable signs that other transformations of the same character are about to take place in the vast empire of China, and in all those countries where inhabitants of different race, yellow, red, or black, are brought into close contact with the men of our own Aryano - Greco - Latin civilization. So vanishes that oft-repeated assertion of the ethnologists, that 

race

 is a final and irreducible fact, and that no possible progress in the perception of scientific or moral truths can ever prevail against it. It is from this point of view that the recent history of the Far East presents phenomena to which it behooves us to devote our most serious attention. 




 There are those, of course, who tell us that all these events are illusory; that the prodigious changes which have taken place in the Japanese world are a lying phantasmagoria and a vain show; that the national mind and character have undergone no real modification; and that the Japanese are sure to escape, sooner or later, from the sphere of European attraction. We hear them compared to savages, who, having learned in the schools of London or Paris the customs of civilization, make haste, as soon as they get back to their forests and savannas, to cast aside their conventional garments, and array themselves in the toggery consecrated by ancestral instinct and hereditary custom. 




 Such assertions appear to us to rest on a complete misconception of indisputable facts. The Japanese have most certainly entered into that realm of civilization on which Bacon and Darwin have set their seal; for if imperial caprice and the spread of bourgeois fashions have power to alter the external aspect of a nation, such influences can have but little effect on its underlying moral sense, its religious beliefs, its educational theories, and the essential principle of its institutions. But it is precisely these “foundations of society” which we have seen removed. Japan has been shaken to the very roots of its political and social being, and agents other than fashion or caprice have been called into play. Is not the suppression of the feudal system, and the substitution for it of a bourgeois organization after the European model, a fact of capital importance? And how complete were the changes effected is shown by the fact that they entailed a formidable reaction, and had to be confirmed by domestic wars, revolutions and counter-revolutions. The resistance of the 

daimyo

, or feudal lords, and of the 

samurai

, or lesser noblemen, continued for fifteen years, and assumed the proportions of a magnificent epic; while the shock of contact between the two societies was so violent as ultimately to shatter all the traditional moulds handed down from the Middle Ages.

A Note on This Standalone Copy An Anarchist Mother's Ache first appeared in an anthology published by Bacchus Editions shortly after the arrest of Luigi Mangione. At the time, we invited writers to respond from whatever vantage point they felt compelled to write, and the result was a collection of very different voices, reflections, and arguments. This essay was my own contribution. Since its publication, I have been asked many times if this final section could be made available on its own. Readers wanted to pass it from hand to hand, carry it in a pocket, or share it without the larger volume. So here it is, now printed as a small standalone pamphlet. It remains exactly as it was originally written, in the midst of the familiar chorus of commentators anxiously debating whether Mangione was politically acceptable enough to embrace, condemn, or distance themselves from. Source

Introduction




 I'm at my favorite café, seated outdoors with the ocean waves as my backdrop, captivated by a man busking with a battered yet beautiful typewriter. Its rhythmic clatter blends seamlessly with his anarchic energy, his wild gestures, and his daring style. 




 Something about him stirs my thoughts, circling me back to the case of Luigi Mangione, a fellow vilified as much for his assumed politics and privilege as for the murder of a CEO. 




 The setting before me compels me to write about the dualities of motherhood and anarchist rebellion. 




Éternel combat de l'amour !




A Mother's Heart and the Anarchist Deed




 To speak of 

propagande par le fait

 is to summon both thrill and mournful reflection, like a mother hearing the distant toll of a funeral bell while her child dances in the garden. 




 Historically, propaganda of the deed has been fraught with as much passion as misunderstanding, willfully misunderstood not only by those outside but also by those within anarchism. From the fevered brilliance of Luigi Galleani's writings in Cronaca Sovversiva to the echo of bullets in Sacco and Vanzetti's America, the deed has been both lionized and damned. 




L'Art de la Révolte




 To be clear, propaganda of the deed is not mere destruction but a creative act: the birth of shocking alarm to awaken slumbering masses. Galleani, whose works danced with dynamite and uncompromising beauty, saw the deed as the poetics of annihilation, an art form that speaks to the heart, bypassing the majority's "reason." For the Galleanists, the deed was not merely a strike against tyranny but a beacon of courage, illuminating paths to freedom for the oppressed. 




Pour moi,

 the tragedy of 

le geste anarchiste

 lies not in its violence but in its reception, mangled by statist propaganda and misunderstood by a public still shackled to the rigid moral framework of the bourgeoisie. 




 To understand the current Luigi, one must first disentangle the romanticized past from the brutal present. This brutal present is one defined by an unprecedented chasm between the corporate elite (backed by the state) and the struggling masses, a society in which corporate monstrosities dictate the terms of existence. It is a time when health itself has been commodified, with medical CEOs profiting obscenely from illness, leaving the vulnerable abandoned in their callous system. Capitalism marches on with predatory tactics, from planned obsolescence to algorithmic manipulation, squeezing every ounce of profit from the exploited. Surveillance, that not-so-silent oppressor, pervades every corner of life, reducing freedom to a quaint memory as the state and corporations collaborate to monitor, control, and, yes, abandon you. 




 As a reminder, the architects of this grim present continue to thrive behind guarded, gilded walls. 




Class Politics: Une Médiocrité Morale!




 The enigmatic, wealthy Mangione replacing the impoverished, laboring immigrant wielding dynamite to demand dignity is, apparently, a contradiction too far for some of today's "anarchists." Perhaps they fail to grasp the truth of rebellion: the deed is not about class, creed, or conformity. 




 Here, I must pause to cast aside the weighty banalities of class politics with a haughty flick of my wrist. The obsession with 

conscience de classe

, with the proletariat as some sacred monolith, leaves me uninterested and cold. The dogma of class struggle, always heavily draped in the tedium of liberalism and Marxist rhetoric, is an insult to the freedom of the individual. 




 Let these groups chatter endlessly about collective liberation; I remain unmoved. 




Pourquoi?

 Because class consciousness demands I prioritize a fabricated identity over my unique Self. It presumes to subsume my desires, my rebellion, my Self into the faceless mass of "the people.” But I am not "the people" nor part of their dull and tacky machinery. I am 

moi-même

 and will never exchange my sovereign ego for their phantom of solidarity. 




 Class struggle is merely the avatar of morality, a hierarchy of its own, demanding allegiance to a collective identity, which is always the lowest common denominator. 




 Does it matter to me whether Luigi Mangione was rich or poor, privileged or oppressed? Not in the least. To frame his deed through the lens of class politics is to diminish its essence. 

L'acte se suffit à lui-même.




 In an age where rebellion is dissected through the lens of identity and ideology, Luigi Mangione offers a stark reminder that the essence of the deed transcends these constructs. 




Mangione: The Formerly Wealthy Pariah




 Luigi Mangione, a young man who, for a time anyway, walked amongst the elite and had access to the type of wealth that insulates one from the suffering that, historically, bred anarchists, stands accused of a deed that ignites shock and admiration. The CEO's murder was swift and executed with the precision of one unburdened by doubt. 




 And yet, I am reading various people in the circle-a world, of all places, arguing over his legacy. 




 Some want to dismiss him outright, citing his privilege, his so-called "heterodox" or "grey" politics, or his failure to articulate an anarchist framework for his act. "He doesn't understand history; he is NOT an anarchist," one complained… as if the dynamite of Galleani or the bombs of Ravachol were wielded by scholars instead of human beings driven to the edge by their desires.

 TO THE PEOPLES OF THE WORLD: 




 TO THE PEOPLE WHO STRUGGLE IN THE FIVE CONTINENTS: 




 BROTHERS AND SISTERS AND COMRADES: 







 In these past months we have established contact among ourselves through various means. We are women, lesbians, gay, transgender, transvestites, intersex, queer and more, men, groups, collectives, associations, organizations, social movements, first peoples, neighbor associations, communities and a long 

et cetera

 that identifies us. 




 We are differentiated and separated by lands, skies, mountains, valleys, steppes, jungles, deserts, oceans, lakes, rivers, streams, lagoons, race, cultures, languages, histories, age, geographies, sexual and non-sexual identities, roots, borders, forms of organization, social classes, purchasing power, social prestige, fame, popularity, followers, likes, coinage, degree of education, ways of being, chores, virtues, defects, pros, cons, howevers, rivalries, enmities, conceptions, arguments, counter-arguments, debates, disputes, denunciations, accusations, disdains, phobias, philias, praises, repudiations, jeers, applause, divinities, demons, dogmas, heresies, joys, dislikes, modes, and a long 

et cetera

 that makes us different and, not infrequently, opposites. 




 We are united only in a few things: 




 In that we make the Earth’s sorrows our own: the violence against women; the persecution and contempt for those different in their affective, emotional, sexual identity; the annihilation of childhood; the genocide against the First Peoples; racism; militarism; exploitation; spoliation; nature’s destruction. 




 The understanding that it is a system which is responsible for these sorrows. The executioner is an exploiting, patriarchal, pyramidal, racist, thieving and criminal system: Capitalism. 




 The knowledge that it is not possible to reform, educate, allay, soften, domesticate, or humanize this system. 




 The commitment to fight, everywhere and at all times —each in their own field— against this system until it is completely destroyed. Humanity’s survival depends on Capitalism’s destruction. We do not surrender, we do not sell out and we do not waver. 




 The certainty that the struggle for Humanity is global. Just as the ongoing destruction recognizes no borders, nationalities, flags, tongues, cultures, races; so, too, is the struggle for Humanity everywhere, at all times. 




 The conviction that many worlds live and fight in The World. And that all pretense of homogeneity and hegemony threatens the human being’s essence: Liberty. Humanity’s equality lies in respecting the different. Its resemblance lies in its diversity. 




 The understanding that it is not the vanity of imposing our gaze, our steps, company, paths and fates what allows us to advance, but rather listening and the sight of the other who, distinct and different, has the same calling to liberty and justice. 




 Due to these convergences, and without abandoning our convictions nor leaving behind who and what we are, we have agreed: 




 First ‒ To realize gatherings, dialogues, exchanging of ideas, experiences, analysis and evaluations amongst the committed we find —from among different conceptions and in different lands— in the struggle for life. Afterwards, each will continue on their own path, or not. Seeing and listening to the other may or may not help us on our way. But to learn of the different is also part of our struggle and our commitment, of our humanity. 




 Second ‒ That these gatherings and activities take place in the five continents. That, with regards to the European continent, these take place in the months of July, August, September and October of the year 2021 with the active participation of a Mexican delegation made up of CNI-CIG, the People’s Front in Defense of the Water and Land of Morelos, Puebla and Tlaxcala, and EZLN. And in later dates to be determined, to support, according to our ability, so that they may be realized in Asia, Africa, Oceania, and America. 




 Third ‒ To invite those who share the same concerns and similar struggles, every honest peoples and all those 

belows

 who rebel and resist in the many corners of the world, so that they join, contribute, support and participate in these gatherings and activities; and so that they may sign off on and make their own this declaration FOR LIFE. 




 From one of the bridges of dignity that joins the five continents. 




 We. 




 Planet Earth.
